sample_answers: The __io_putchar function is required in embedded systems because the printf function does not know by default where to send the output. It usually expects an output stream, which does not exist in microcontrollers. Implement this function helps us define how and where each character from printf should be sent (e.g. UART). This allows printf to be used in embedded systems by routing output to hardware-specific interfaces. Without __io_putchar there would be no output from printf, since there’s no default output in most embedded environments.\n

The __io_putchar function sends a single character to a hardware peripheral, usually UART, allowing printf to display output in embedded systems. It’s needed because embedded devices don’t have standard output by default, so programmers must implement this function to define how characters are transmitted, typically over serial communication.\n

__io_putchar pushes a character over the UART interface (using HAL_UART_Transmit), it then returns the same character. This method is used by printf() in order to help us send data over UART. This allows us to monitor variables and/or logs that the microcontroller has during runtime. Based off the fact that __io_putchar uses “IO” instead of “UART”, this method is probably overloaded depending on the target system in order to provide printf() or any other a method to output characters. For example, you might overload __io_putchar to push a character into stream instead of UART on your personal computer; it depends on the platform. The return type of __io_putchar is to just verify that it has succeeded, it is not the main reason the function exists and is for error checking.\n

The __io_putchar function is meant to send a single character to the uart2 I/O channel. The function then returns this letter so that the printf function can output them as a string to the output channel. The __io_putchar function specifically allows the programmer to select which output is used, if this was part of a standard library than the programmer wouldn’t be able to do this. This allows the programmer to better test that certain features are being used correctly.\n

__io_putchar acts as a wrapper function that is called by the printf function to output individual characters to the UART or console. Since the printf function is part of the stdio library, which is designed for general-purpose systems, a wrapper like __io_putchar is necessary to bridge the gap between the library and the hardware-specific input/output channel.\n

The _io_putchar function is a return function that returns the very same character that was inputted as it’s char parameter. This is a needed function especially when using printf, as it calls the _io_putchar function multiple times to print out the desired input string. Another reason why the _io_putchar function is required to be implemented is because the <stdio.h> library, where the printf function comes from is mainly reliant on these helper functions to allow it to interact with various kinds of hardware that provide different configurations of the output. The _io_putchar function is interpreted differently for each type of hardware so that the printf function can flexibly function.\n

While printf is normally used to print output to a console, it is a part of the stdio.h library. This entire library relies on helper functions to interact with the hardware, meaning printf can’t directly interact with hardware by itself. The __io_putchar uses a function HAL_URT_Transmit that “puts” a character into the specified output channel (in this case it is UART2, a peripheral set up by the HAL used to print from the MCU to the PC), and is repeatedly called by printf to print all the characters in the string passed to it. Finally, because the function works using the HAL, the underlying hardware can be changed without needing to change the user code. The HAL provides a generic base to interact with many different types of hardware, which allows this function to still be applicable across many different devices. Modifying this function allows redirection of output to other devices, such as USB or an LCD, making it an essential component in adapting standard output functions for embedded environments.\n

The __io_putchar function takes a character input (a 1-byte variable representing any value defined in the ASCII table of codes, characters, and symbols) and internally calls the HAL_UART_Transmit function to send that character over the Nucleo board’s primary UART interface. This is achieved by passing &huart2 as the UART handler to the HAL_UART_Transmit function.
